problem.title: Two Sum II - Input Array Is Sorted
problem.description: The list numbers is sorted from smallest to largest. Find the two different positions whose values add up to target. Return them counted from 1 (the first item is position 1), smaller position first. There is always exactly one answer, and you may only use a constant amount of extra memory.

examples.note: Negative numbers work the same way.

constraints: numbers is sorted in non-decreasing order.
Exactly one pair adds up to target.

solutionSummaries.name: Fix one, binary search the other

solutions.name: Check every pair
solutions.complexityWhy: For each of the n numbers, the inner loop tries every number after it: about n²/2 sums. Only a few index variables are stored.
solutions.bottleneck: It never uses the fact that the list is sorted, so it checks pairs that the order already rules out.
solutions.insight: The list is sorted. Once you fix the first number, you know exactly which value you need, and a sorted list can be searched for a value in O(log n).

steps.note: n = 6 numbers. The plan: try every pair (i, j) with i before j.
1 + 11 = 12. Not 10. Every pair with 1 has failed.
i = 1: the value 3. j starts again right after i.
3 + 11 = 14. Not 10. It kept going after the sums passed 10, even though in a sorted list they could only grow.
Return [3, 4]. The answer counts positions from 1, so add 1 to each index. That took 10 sums here.

solutions.name: Fix one, binary search the other
solutions.complexityWhy: For each of the n numbers, a binary search over the rest takes O(log n) steps. It only keeps a few index variables.
solutions.bottleneck: Every new first number starts a fresh search from scratch, even though the previous searches already told you a lot.
solutions.insight: Look at the smallest and largest values together. If their sum is too small, the smallest value can't be in the answer; if it's too big, the largest can't. One sum rules out one value, so two pointers finish in O(n).

steps.note: Search for 9 only after i: indexes lo = 1 to hi = 5.
lo ≤ hi: the range isn't empty yet.
Look in the middle: mid = (1 + 5) // 2 = 3, the value 6.
6 is less than 9, so 9 can only be to the right of mid.
Throw away the left half: lo = 4.
lo ≤ hi: keep searching indexes 4 to 5.
So 9 could only be to the left: hi = 4.
lo > hi: the range is empty. There is no 9, so 1 is not in the answer.
lo > hi: empty. There is no 7, so 3 is not in the answer.
Return [3, 4]: indexes 2 and 3, counted from 1. Each search halves its range, so it takes O(log n) looks instead of n.

solutions.name: Two pointers from both ends
solutions.complexityWhy: Every pass of the loop moves left right or right left by one, and they stop when they meet: at most n − 1 moves. Only two indexes are stored.
solutions.insight: This is the same walk as the sort-then-two-pointers idea for Two Sum, minus the sort. A hash map would also be O(n), but it uses O(n) memory, which this problem doesn't allow.

steps.note: Put left on the smallest value (1) and right on the largest (11).
left is before right, so there are pairs to try.
12 is not less than 10: too big. 11 is too big even with the smallest value, 1. Drop 11.
right moves to 8. The value 11 is ruled out.
left is still before right: keep going.
9 is less than 10: too small. 8 is now the largest value left, so 1 can never reach 10. Drop 1.
11 is not less than 10: too big. Drop 8.
9 is less than 10: too small. Drop 3.
Return [3, 4], counted from 1. 5 sums instead of 10, and no extra memory.
